cells.tense: You're tending what's yours right now, and your hands are open about it.
cells.ask: Let one effort finish before you name what it made — say the good thing it did out loud to whoever it served.
cells.core:
The tending is steady and your hands aren't clenched around it. You know what you're responsible for, you give it what it needs, and when something has carried itself far enough you set it down without a fight. The care doesn't leave when your hands do. People around you feel that steadiness, and things get handed forward because you handed them, not because you held on.

Letting go is the last move of good tending, not a loss you're absorbing. When an effort finishes, say what it made while it still has your voice on it, and the acknowledgment turns the release into something worth having done rather than something you simply survive.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's yours and open your hands when it's done.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: in the letting go that clears space for what's worth keeping

cells.tense: You're already three seasons past where you actually stand.
cells.ask: Name what this effort gave you now, before it's finished — let the satisfaction land where you are instead of saving it for a harvest you keep pushing back.
cells.core:
Tending something well and letting it grow at its own pace looks quiet from the outside. You put it in the ground, you give it water, you wait for the season to do its part — and because you're resting on what's actually here, the care stays steady and doesn't exhaust you. The work gets your hands, not your whole forward-leaning weight.

You're carrying the future version instead, and carrying it hard. Before anyone asks, before anything is done, you're already hauling what comes next — watering a field you haven't planted. Care that doesn't exhaust comes from holding what's growing without clutching at what you haven't grown yet. Say what this gave you today and let that be enough for now.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending what hasn't grown yet and missing what's here.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: in the letting go that clears space for what's worth keeping

cells.tense: You've set the work down some time back and you're still not picking it up.
cells.ask: Put one small thing back in the ground — not because you feel like it, but because you're still the one who knows how to tend it.
cells.core:
The tending is quiet and ongoing when it's working. You put things in the ground, you look after them, and when something finishes you open your hands and let it go without a fight. The hope that keeps that running doesn't need to be loud or dramatic. It just needs to keep showing up, and it does, mostly without you noticing it.

You've stopped. The tending went quiet somewhere, and the open hands that used to come after a finished job haven't shown up in a while — so things sit almost finished, and what's worth passing on sits unpassed. It isn't that you don't care. Keep hoping out loud for one small thing, and the strength for the work comes back through the hoping itself. Pick one thing up.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped tending, and the hope that drives it went with it.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: in the letting go that clears space for what's worth keeping

cells.tense: You're already releasing things, and you've been calling it something other than your own doing.
cells.ask: Say out loud what one of those releases cost you — the letting go that looked easy — and let someone besides yourself call it what it was.
cells.core:
Finishing something and knowing it was you who finished it — that's the healthy shape here. You let go of what's used up, you make room for what's next, and you can point at the releasing as your own move. The hands doing it are yours, and that's plain to you and plain to whoever watched you do it.

That part is missing. The releasing has been happening already — things closed out, space cleared — and it gets described as if it happened on its own. Nobody has confirmed the letting go as yours, so the credit never lands where it actually belongs. Letting go is the completion of care, and completions want a witness. Tell one person what one of those quiet releases cost you, and pointing at it is what makes it feel like something you chose rather than something that swept past you.
cells.sheetLine: You're already letting go. You haven't said it's yours.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: in the letting go that clears space for what's worth keeping
